newsitem.title: USA: Chinese envoy urges deeper U.S. ties with Beijing.
newsitem.headline: Chinese envoy urges deeper U.S. ties with Beijing.

text.p: China's ambassador called on the United States on Friday to seize what he termed a historic opportunity to work more closely together for the good of world peace.

Citing a series of high-level U.S. visits to Beijing, beginning on Monday with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Ambassador Li Daoyu said: "We believe it is time both China and the United States increase dialogue and enlarge cooperation."

"It is time both countries meet the challenge of history and work to bring a stable, healthy Sino-U.S. relationship into the 21st century," he told a symposium marking the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Communique that set the stage for normal diplomatic ties in 1979.

The ambassador referred to the scheduled visit late next month of Vice President Al Gore, which is designed to pave the way for an exchange of visits between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin in the next two years.
However, Gore's office said on Friday that no date had been set for his visit.
The ambassador quoted the late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, who died on Wednesday, as having attached great importance to developing Sino-U.S. ties in the interest of world peace.

"Of course, we still have differences, as we did 25 years ago," he said. The future of Taiwan, which Beijing considers a renegade province, is the "most important and sensitive" point of contention, the ambassador said.

"To properly handle the Taiwan issue holds the key to a stable Sino-U.S. relationship," he said. He said the issue should be dealt with according to principles laid out in the Shanghai Communique, in which Beijing and Washingnton agreed on a "one China" policy with respect to Taiwan, and two companion joint communiques.

"Only when these principles are observed ... can we avoid the interference of the Taiwan issue with China-U.S. relations and ensure a stable bilateral relationship," Li Daoyu added at the symposium. It was sponsored by the U.S.-China Policy Foundation, a private grouping that includes many old U.S. China hands.

U.S. ties with China went into a tailspin from which they only emerged late last year after Clinton let President Lee Teng-Hui of Taiwan enter the United States to attend a college reunion in June 1995. No other Taiwan head of state had been granted an entry visa since the United States downgraded relations with Taiwan in 1979.
The ambassador said the United States and China shared strategic interests in promoting peace, stability and prosperity in the Asia Pacific area and throughout the world.
Each has an important stake in expanding bilateral trade and economic cooperation, he added. "And both face the same challenge: to combat transnational problems such as environmental pollution."
"In fact, history has given our two countries a remarkable opportunity to work closer together," he said.
